item.title: Living in Dizzasco and working in Ticino as a border worker
item.description: Practical guide for border workers: G permit, taxes, AVS/LPP, LAMal, refreshments, travel times and cost of living between Dizzasco and Ticino.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- New Cross-Border Agreement effective from 1 January 2024 - Exemption €7,500 (old) and €10,000 (new cross-border workers) - Withholding tax deducted only in Switzerland - Permit G to work daily in the Canton of Ticino
## Key facts
- **What**: Living in Lombardy and working as a cross-border commuter in Swiss Ticino - When: New agreement from 1 January 2024 - Where: Dizzasco, Chiasso and Brogeda border crossings towards Ticino - Who: Cross-border workers category G with employment in Switzerland - Exemption: €7,500 (old), €10,000 (new from 17 July 2023) - Convention: 9 December 1976 (double taxation)
### The New Cross-Border Agreement and status from 2024
From 1 January 2024, the New Cross-Border Agreement between Switzerland and Italy has come into effect, modifying the tax and social security rules for those living in Dizzasco and Italy and working in the Canton of Ticino. The agreement was signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy through Law 83 of 13 June 2023. For a cross-border worker residing in this area of Lombardy, this is a milestone that simplifies the tax regime and offers new advantages.
The withholding tax on employment income is deducted exclusively in Switzerland and managed by the AFC (Federal Tax Administration) based on the rates of the Canton of Ticino. Italy does not apply a parallel deduction. This means that the cross-border worker does not suffer immediate double taxation on their pay slip. The Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976 regulates the tax credit: by declaring the income in Italy through the CE section of the income tax return (model 730), the Revenue Agency recognizes the taxes already paid in Switzerland, avoiding overlaps.
The distinction between old and new cross-border workers is crucial and direct. Those who were already cross-border workers before 17 July 2023 benefit from an exemption of €7,500 annually on the Italian taxable income, with a transitional regime extended until 2033. Those who acquired the status of cross-border worker after that date are entitled to a more generous exemption of €10,000 annually. This exemption significantly lowers the Italian taxable base and reduces the IRPEF due (23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000).
### Permit G and the Dizzasco-Ticino connection
To work daily in the Canton of Ticino, the cross-border worker residing in Dizzasco needs the permit G (cross-border worker permit), issued by the Swiss authorities (SEM — State Secretariat for Migration) in coordination with the Ticino cantonal authorities. The proximity of Dizzasco to the Chiasso and Brogeda border crossings makes daily commuting practical. The permit allows crossing the border every day to go to work. It is the Swiss employer who requests the permit and demonstrates that the position cannot be filled by Swiss residents. ## Taxes, Double Taxation, and Tax Credit
Living in Dizzasco means navigating two parallel tax systems: the Swiss system of Switzerland (where you work) and the Italian system (where you reside). The logic of the Convention of December 9, 1976 is to prevent the same income from being taxed twice in full.
The Swiss withholding tax is deducted by the employer based on the federal, cantonal, and municipal rates of the Canton of Ticino, and typically ranges from 15% to 25% of the gross income. However, the Italian cross-border worker must still file an income tax return in Italy, where the income is taxed according to the IRPEF: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000. Without protection, the income would be subject to full double taxation. The solution is the tax credit, recognized on the CE section of the 730 declaration: the amount of Swiss tax already paid is deducted from the Italian IRPEF. Since the Swiss rates are generally lower, the cross-border worker often receives a positive amount (the tax refund) from the Revenue Agency, typically paid between April and June.
### AVS, LPP, and Italian Pension System: The Double Pension System
In Switzerland, the cross-border worker is required to contribute to three pillars of pension. The AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) and AI (Disability Insurance) together with the IPG (loss of earnings allowance) absorb 5.3% of the gross salary as an employee contribution (the employer contributes the same amount). The Unemployment Insurance (AD) and Accident Insurance (AC) add 1.1% (up to CHF 148,200 of salary), the LAINF (occupational accident insurance) 0.7–1.5%, and the LPP (occupational pension scheme, second pillar) varies from 7% to 18% depending on age (from 25 years onwards) and the company.
In parallel, the cross-border worker remains registered with the INPS for the mandatory Italian pension system. The new agreement of 2024 clarifies that the contributions paid in Switzerland (AVS and LPP) are fully recognized by Italy for the calculation of future pensions. There are no losses: the cross-border worker accumulates a pension position that combines Swiss and Italian contributions, coordinated by the International Convention.
### LAMal, Costs, and Insurance Choices
The Swiss health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for cross-border workers in category G. Unlike Swiss residents, the cross-border worker has the option to choose: to be insured in Switzerland or to remain in the Italian healthcare system if already covered by a spouse or another family member. The Swiss adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually depending on the policy. The cost of LAMal is fully deductible from the Swiss taxable base, effectively reducing the withholding tax. Choosing Swiss LAMal with a low deductible (CHF 300) results in a higher monthly premium but greater protection.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## Operating procedure: from G permit to net calculation
### Step 1: G permit and Swiss registration
The first concrete step is for the Swiss employer to request the G permit from the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration). The procedure typically takes 1–2 months. Once approved, the cross-border worker receives the physical permit valid for one year, renewable. At the same time, the cross-border worker must register with the municipality of Dizzasco as a cross-border worker and obtain the Swiss tax identification number (SIN), necessary for the Italian declaration.
### Step 2: Income tax declaration and CE form
Every year by May 31, the cross-border worker must submit the Italian income tax declaration (model 730 or Redditi Persone Fisiche). The Swiss employer provides the tax certificate (CU) by February, with income data and taxes already withheld. The cross-border worker must complete the CE form of the declaration, reporting the Swiss income declared and the Swiss tax paid. The Revenue Agency automatically recognizes the tax credit, calculating any positive refunds.
### Step 3: Net calculation and simulation
The monthly net depends on the gross salary, the Ticino withholding tax rate, social security contributions, health insurance, and family status. An estimate for a gross salary of CHF 4,500 might involve a total deduction (taxes + AVS/AI/IPG/AD/AC/LPP/LAINF/LAMal contributions) around 25–30%, leaving a net of about CHF 3,100–3,375. This figure varies considerably based on the municipality of residence, the canton, the number of children, and the choice of LAMal.
Using the [dedicated online calculator](nav:calculator) for cross-border workers allows you to simulate the net salary by entering personal data (marital status, children, gross income, LAMal choice). The tool applies the updated federal and Ticino cantonal rates and provides a realistic estimate.
### Step 4: Tax refund and deadlines
The refund is the reimbursement that the Revenue Agency recognizes when the Swiss tax is lower than the Italian IRPEF due. It is calculated on the 730 declaration and paid between April and June to the taxpayer's account. Typical amounts range from a few hundred to a few thousand euros annually. Always keep Swiss documents (tax certificates, statements from SIA or the employer) to support the declared tax credit.
### Step 5: Assistance and tools
Consulting a tax advisor or accountant specializing in cross-border workers is recommended to optimize your overall position. Platforms like [the cross-border calculator](nav:calculator) and resources dedicated to [refunds](nav:ristorni) help manage deadlines and understand the orders of magnitude of your annual net and expected refunds.

Living in Cassina Rizzardi and working in Ticino is a popular choice among border workers: the municipality of Como is a few kilometers from the Ticino border, allows you to maintain roots in the Italian territory and access the Swiss labour market with significantly higher salaries. What does it mean concretely from a fiscal, social security and logistical point of view?
The figure of the frontier worker — category G for cross-border workers — is regulated by the New Frontier Agreement signed on 23 December 2020, which entered into force on 1 January 2024. This agreement has significantly changed taxation and social security contributions, with direct impacts on the monthly paycheck.
### Set ### Cost of living: Cassina Rizzardi vs. Ticino
Moving from a Comasco municipality to Ticino involves significant considerations regarding housing costs, utilities, food, and services. Cassina Rizzardi generally offers lower costs compared to Ticino municipalities such as Lugano, Bellinzona, or Mendrisio. This is one of the main advantages of maintaining residency in Italy while working in Switzerland.
**Real Estate and Rentals**: Cassina Rizzardi offers houses for rent and sale at lower prices compared to the Ticino market. Those who buy in Italy use the euro, while a potential mortgage in Swiss francs would involve exchange rate exposure. Many cross-border commuters choose to rent in Italy (lower rent) and work in Ticino for this economic reason.
Utilities: Electricity, gas, and internet in Italy follow rates regulated by the Italian market, generally lower than in Switzerland. Moving to Ticino would result in significantly higher energy costs.
Groceries and Daily Expenses: Living in Cassina Rizzardi allows access to Italian prices for food shopping, stores, and services. Many cross-border commuters maintain this base to control their monthly budget, resorting to Ticino only for specialized purchases or services not available.
Use the [Ticino vs. Italy cost of living comparator](nav:cost-of-living) for a personalized estimate: enter data on family, rent, consumption, and you will get the monthly spending difference between living in Cassina Rizzardi and moving to Ticino.
### Commuting and Border Crossings
The distance between Cassina Rizzardi and the main Ticino work centers (Lugano, Chiasso, Mendrisio, Bellinzona) is short. By car, the journey takes about 30-45 minutes depending on the destination and traffic conditions at the border crossings.
The main border crossings for those living in the Comasco area: - Brogeda (Como-Ticino): a minor crossing, less congested during peak hours - Chiasso (Como-Ticino): the main one, often congested in the morning and afternoon during commuting hours - Gaggiolo (Varese-Ticino): an alternative for those working in the Locarnese area (Locarno, Ascona, Tenero)
Many cross-border commuters choose public transport (trains from Como to Chiasso, then Ticino buses/trains) to avoid traffic, gasoline, and parking costs in Ticino. The option of partial telecommuting further reduces the number of commuting days per week.
### LAMal: Choosing Health Insurance
The cross-border commuter category G resident in Italy has the right to choose between Swiss health insurance (LAMal) or maintaining the Italian INPS/SSN system.
Most opt for LAMal as it offers comprehensive coverage, quick response times, and direct access to Ticino and Swiss hospitals. Annual premiums are substantial, but the coverage is complete. LAMal includes deductibles for adults ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 depending on the chosen policy.
Those who choose the Italian system must maintain local INPS registration and receive Italian health coverage with lower contribution costs. The decision depends on personal evaluations of preferred healthcare quality, desired coverage, and cost-benefit.

In addition to AVS and LPP (mandatory), the cross-border commuter can subscribe to a 3rd Pillar (3a) to accumulate additional pension savings with Swiss tax advantages. The maximum annual contributions are set by Swiss federal regulations and are deducted from taxable income in the canton of work. This is an optional but recommended tool to increase future pension income.
### Double Taxation: How the Tax Credit Works
The Italy-Switzerland Convention of December 9, 1976 prevents the same income from being taxed in both countries. The concrete mechanism: 1. Switzerland applies withholding tax (deducted by the employer) 2. Italy does not apply additional taxation on foreign employment income 3. In the Italian model 730 (section CE), the cross-border commuter declares Swiss income and requests the tax credit 4. If Swiss withholdings exceed Italian taxes due, a refund is generated via the 730
This architecture eliminates the double taxation that would characterize a separate national taxation regime.

Step 1: Job offer and employer's request The Ticino employer submits a G permit request for the foreign worker to the competent cantonal offices (usually the Migration Section or the Department of Justice of the Canton of Ticino). The procedure typically takes 4-8 weeks. The costs are borne by the employer.
Step 2: Registration and declaration of foreign income The worker registers their residence in Cassina Rizzardi at the local town hall as a resident working in Switzerland. They must complete a future income declaration according to the forms required by the Swiss and Italian authorities.
Step 3: Registration with tax authorities Once the G permit is obtained: - **In Switzerland**: the employer registers them with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV) in the canton where the company is located. The cross-border worker receives a Swiss tax identification number (IDE). - In Italy: the worker registers the new foreign employment income with the Como province section of the Revenue Agency. This registration allows the declaration of Swiss income in the annual 730 form and the request for tax credit.
Step 4: Opening a bank account and salary payment The employer makes salary payments via bank transfer. The cross-border worker opens (or uses) an Italian bank account to receive the payments. Some also maintain a Swiss bank account for withdrawals in CHF or payment of pension contributions.
### Pre-move checklist: verify these points
Before moving to Cassina Rizzardi with the intention of working in Ticino, mark the following as completed: - ✅ Valid Italian identity document (passport or electronic ID card) - ✅ Job offer letter from the Ticino employer with start date and gross annual salary - ✅ Availability for change of residence registration in Cassina Rizzardi - ✅ Choice of Swiss LAMal (or confirmation of Italian health system) - ✅ Opening an Italian bank account (or verification of availability with the current bank) - ✅ Information on the composition of gross salary, Swiss withholdings, and net monthly amount - ✅ Contact details of the tax consultant for the 730 declaration with foreign income

This simulation allows you to evaluate whether the Swiss salary, net of taxes and contributions, compensates for the Italian cost of living and justifies daily commuting to the border crossings. Combine the [calculator](nav:calculator) with the cost of living comparator for a complete evaluation.
### Critical annual deadlines for the cross-border worker
After the first year of work, the cross-border worker must comply with precise administrative deadlines: - May 31: Deadline for the Italian 730 declaration (previous year's income with CE form and tax credit) - March 15 (indicative): Deadline for communicating income data to the FTA/ESTV if requested by the canton - January: Receipt of pay slip with annual withholding certificate (necessary for the 730) - By January 31 of the following year: The cantonal administration communicates the final withholdings paid
Failure to comply with the 730 deadlines results in administrative penalties in Italy. Consultation with a tax accountant specializing in cross-border workers is recommended for the first two years.

For specific clarifications on the G permit, taxation, AVS/LPP, and LAMal: 1. Contact the Ticino employer (human resources office) to verify the permit request process 2. Contact the competent cantonal migration office of Ticino (usually the Migration Section, Department of Justice) 3. Contact the Como province section of the Revenue Agency for registration as a foreign employee 4. Request a quote from a LAMal insurer to evaluate premiums and deductibles 5. Use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) for an initial estimate of the net pay slip 6. Consult a tax accountant specializing in Ticino-Italy cross-border workers for a personalized evaluation of convenience and the 730 procedure

item.title: Accident in progress: LAINF complaint for border workers
item.description: LAINF covers injuries on the commute to the border. Here's what's different about a trip and how to file a report.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - LAINF covers accidents on the way to work up to the Swiss border - Report to SUVA if the accident occurs in Switzerland - Crucial difference: regular commute ≠ extraordinary business trip
## Key facts - **What**: Accident insurance coverage (LAINF) for cross-border commuters at the border - Managing entity: SUVA (Switzerland) if the accident occurs in Swiss territory - Alternative coverage: INPS (Italy) if the accident occurs beyond the border - Difference: Regular commute always covered; business trip: depends on circumstances - Where: Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo crossings; A2 routes, regional roads
A cross-border commuter who suffers an accident on the way from home to work is entitled to Swiss LAINF coverage. But what happens if the accident occurs at the Brogeda, Chiasso crossing, or beyond the border? And how to differentiate a claim for a regular commute from one for a business trip? The distinction is crucial as it determines which regulations apply and which entity manages the compensation.
### When LAINF coverage applies
The LAINF (Federal Law on Accident Insurance) in Switzerland automatically covers employed workers. For a cross-border commuter with a G permit who resides in Canton Ticino and works in Italy, the protection depends on where the accident occurs.
If the accident happens during the commute before crossing the Swiss border — for example, on the road from Chiasso to the company in Lombardy — Swiss LAINF coverage applies, as the worker is still under the jurisdiction of the Swiss insurance system.
Conversely, if the accident occurs in Italian territory, Italian regulations apply, and compensation falls under the jurisdiction of the INPS (National Institute for Social Security).
### Regular commute vs. business trip: the crucial difference
A fundamental aspect for the claim concerns the nature of the trip. A regular commute is the ordinary and repetitive route that the cross-border commuter takes daily from their Ticino home to their usual workplace. A business trip, on the other hand, is an extraordinary journey to a different destination from the usual workplace — a construction site, a branch office, a meeting with a distant client.
This distinction is not formal: it changes the insurance coverage. A regular commute is always covered by LAINF; a business trip to a secondary location might fall into a different category, depending on the specific circumstances.
For the cross-border commuter, it is essential to accurately document the type of trip at the time of the claim, attaching testimonies, photos of the location, times, and statements about the intended destination. ### How the Italian-Swiss Convention Regulates Coverage
The Convention between Italy and Switzerland, in force since December 9, 1976, governs the treatment of cross-border workers in terms of social security and insurance. In the event of an accident at the border, it is this bilateral norm that decides which system covers the incident.
If a cross-border worker with a Permesso G suffers an accident between their Swiss residence and the border crossing — for example, on the A2 in Swiss territory — LAINF responds directly through SUVA. If, however, the accident occurs after Chiasso or Brogeda, even if the worker was still on their way to the company in Italy, it is the Italian work insurance (managed by INPS) that intervenes.
This geographical distinction is sometimes delicate: if the accident occurs exactly at the border or in an ambiguous border area, it is crucial to obtain the report from the Swiss or Italian road police, which precisely attests to the exact location and thus the jurisdiction.
### What Changes for the Ticino Cross-Border Worker
For those working with a Permesso G, the advantage is having LAINF coverage that extends to the border, ensuring protection during the daily 30-60 minute commute. This is particularly relevant because the journey to Italy involves specific risks: delays at border crossings, concentrated traffic, morning queues, overtaking maneuvers in critical areas.
If the accident occurs in Swiss territory, the cross-border worker does not need to contact the Italian company or INPS directly: the report goes to SUVA, which follows the entire procedure according to Swiss law.
If it occurs already in Italy, the protocol changes completely. Here, INPS comes into play, and the cross-border worker must coordinate with the Italian employer to start the procedure with the transalpine social security institute. The times, forms, daily allowance amounts, and level of coverage can differ significantly from the Swiss system.
### Scenario: When the Border is the Limit
Consider a cross-border worker reaching the Brogeda border crossing during rush hour. An accident during this journey will be covered by SUVA, as it occurs in Switzerland and falls within the "home-work" journey under LAINF.
If, however, the same cross-border worker, once they have crossed the border and are already in Italian territory on the provincial road to the company, suffers an accident, the responsibility shifts to the Italian INPS. Here, the compensation will follow Italian criteria and amounts, not Swiss. The Swiss daily allowance and the Italian one can differ significantly, as can the management times of the procedure and the medical checks required.
For this reason, keeping documents that attest to the exact location (witnesses, photos, medical certificates with location, road police report) is essential to protect one's rights and avoid disputes over jurisdiction.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### SUVA reporting procedure: essential steps
If the accident occurred in Swiss territory during the commute to work, the cross-border worker must initiate a reporting procedure with SUVA. The report does not need to be submitted personally by the worker: usually, the employer or the treating physician will transmit it.
Step 1: Immediate notification of the employer. The cross-border worker immediately informs the company of the accident, specifying the time, location (Brogeda, Chiasso, provincial road, etc.), dynamics of the event, and names of any witnesses.
Step 2: Medical care and documentation. If necessary, the cross-border worker seeks medical care (emergency room, clinic, hospital) and carefully keeps all medical certificates, radiological reports, prescriptions, and treatment documentation.
Step 3: Filling out and submitting the SUVA form. The employer (or the treating physician) fills out the official SUVA reporting form and submits it to the insurer within the deadlines set by Swiss law.
Step 4: Investigation and communication of the outcome. SUVA initiates the investigation, requests any clarifications, and communicates the outcome of the coverage, the amounts of daily allowances, and the details of the continuation of the treatment to the cross-border worker.
### Essential documentation to expedite the process
To avoid delays and disputes, the cross-border worker must compile a complete file:
- Written statement of the event (date, exact time, geographical location, dynamics, causes) - Initial medical certificate (first treatment in hospital or clinic with stamp and date) - Photographs of the accident site (if possible, taken within the first few hours) - Names and contacts of witnesses present - Copy of the G Permit and employment contract - Statement of usual destination and regular route - Swiss road police report (if the accident was reported to the authorities)
This documentation is crucial to prove to SUVA that it was a regular commute to work and not an extraordinary trip or deviation from the route.
### When to consult a specialist
If the accident is serious or involves prolonged absences from work, or if SUVA partially denies coverage or requests complex clarifications, the cross-border worker should consult a specialist in labor law or social security law. In Canton Ticino, cross-border worker associations and unions offer free or low-cost consultations.
In addition, if the accident involves the border — for example, if the exact location of the accident is unclear or if the cross-border worker crossed the border shortly before the incident — it is useful to obtain the Swiss road police report, which certifies the location and clarifies the jurisdiction in an irrefutable manner.
### Next steps and useful tools
To verify if your G Permit includes extended LAINF coverage and how it differs from other options, consult the [G Permit vs B comparator](nav:permit-compare) available on the site.
To learn more about Swiss social security rights and insurance rates that protect in case of accident, use the [paycheck calculator](nav:calculator) and check the LAINF percentage applied to your salary.
If you have specific doubts about which legislation applies to your case — Swiss or Italian — or if you wish to have a preliminary assessment of your situation, contact SUVA directly or consult a law firm specializing in cross-border law in Ticino.

item.title: Changing working canton: tax guide
item.description: The transfer from one Swiss canton to another affects permission, taxation and contributions. Learn how the New 2024 Agreement changes the rules.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Permit G remains valid: no renewal required when changing canton - Withholding tax varies by cantonal rates; only deducted in Switzerland - New cross-border commuters: €10,000/year exemption; old €7,500 until 2033 (2024 Agreement) - Modified AVS/LPP contributions: check enrollment in the new canton's funds
## Key facts - **What**: Change of work canton between Ticino, Grisons, or other Swiss cantons - When: Valid from January 1, 2024 (New Cross-Border Agreement) - Where: Swiss territory; identical rules for all cantons bordering Italy - Who: Italy-Switzerland cross-border commuters holding Permit G - Taxation: Withholding tax administered by AFC (Federal Tax Administration) - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee; LPP 7–18% by age group; LAINF 0.7–1.5% - Reference agreement: Double taxation convention Italy-Switzerland (December 9, 1976); New Agreement signed December 23, 2020 - Refunds: Old cross-border commuters (before July 17, 2023) €7,500 exemption; new €10,000 exemption
A cross-border commuter changing work canton in Switzerland faces issues beyond simply signing a new contract. Work permit, taxation, pension contributions, and health coverage require special attention, especially after the New Cross-Border Agreement came into effect on January 1, 2024. This agreement significantly modified the tax regime and refunds for those crossing the Italy-Switzerland border daily, creating new opportunities but also new administrative deadlines.
The 2024 New Agreement distinguishes between "old" cross-border commuters (already such before July 17, 2023) and "new." The former maintain an annual exemption of €7,500 until 2033, while the latter have a €10,000 exemption. These amounts directly affect the Italian tax return (CE section of the 730 form) and the calculation of refunds via tax credit. Changing work canton does not invalidate these rights but requires timely notification to the employer.
### Does the Permit G remain valid when changing canton?
The Permit G certifies the right to work in Switzerland for Italian citizens residing in Italy. Contrary to a common belief, the document is not tied to a specific canton but allows work throughout Swiss territory. If a cross-border commuter changes work canton, the permit remains valid: no new issuance is required from the previous canton's office. However, it is advisable to communicate the change to the employer and ensure they notify the competent authorities (SEM, State Secretariat for Migration). In practice, moving from a company in Ticino to one in Grisons requires only notification to the new employer; the Permit G card does not change. The communication of the change of employer to the SEM is the responsibility of the new employer, who must register the cross-border commuter within eight days of the start of activity.
### How does the withholding tax change between cantons?
The withholding tax on employment income is deducted exclusively in Switzerland — never in both countries. This is guaranteed by the Italy-Switzerland double taxation convention (signed December 9, 1976) and reinforced by the 2024 New Agreement. However, taxation varies based on the work canton: each canton applies different federal and cantonal rates, administered by the AFC (Federal Tax Administration) and cantonal tax offices. Changing canton can therefore lead to a change in the amount deducted from the paycheck, both in terms of the rate and the deductions applied. The difference does not result in double taxation but requires attention to comparing paychecks: the net amount can vary significantly between Ticino and Grisons. For example, federal, cantonal, and municipal rates and personal exemptions differ: it is advisable to ask the new employer for an estimate of the monthly deduction before formalizing the move. ### Impact on Payroll, AVS, and LPP
The transition between cantons modifies the contributions paid for retirement. The AVS/AI/IPG (Old Age-Invalidity-Lost Earnings Insurance) remains at 5.3% for the employee, regardless of the canton, but the employer pays their equal share to the canton of work. The LPP (Supplementary Old Age Insurance), however, is managed by the employer through a pension fund registered in that canton: the percentage contributions vary from 7% to 18% depending on age and the chosen fund. A cross-border worker who moves from an employer in Ticino to one in Graubünden may find themselves enrolled in a different LPP fund, with slightly different rates and, possibly, partially portable acquired rights (depending on the fund's regulations). [Consult our guide on retirement](nav:pension) for details on portable LPP rights.
Contributions for accident insurance (LAINF) and family allowances may also see minimal variations based on the cantons, although they remain around 0.7–1.5% for LAINF. [Check the overall payroll cost](nav:payslip) in the new canton. It is important to ask the new employer for a copy of the enrollment documentation to the funds, verify that previous contributions are correctly credited, and check the first month's payroll for any anomalies. Keep all correspondence between the old and new employer regarding the transfer of LPP rights.
### LAMal (health insurance) and right of option
Cross-border workers with Permit G have the right to choose between Swiss health insurance (LAMal, "Health Insurance Act") and Italian insurance (CMI). Many opt for LAMal because it offers coverage in Switzerland during work and lower deductibles (between CHF 300 and CHF 2500 for adults). A change in the canton of work does not alter the right of option, but it can offer the opportunity to renegotiate the policy: different LAMal companies operate in various cantons with slightly different premiums and coverages. It is advisable to contact the current insurer before moving to communicate the new work address (the canton of work is relevant for premium calculation). If a cross-border worker wants to switch from LAMal to CMI (or vice versa), the change in canton of work is a good time to notify the transition, although it can occur at any time of the year with respect to notice periods.
### Tax refunds and income tax declaration
The New Agreement 2024 has consolidated the figure of the "historic" cross-border worker (already such before July 17, 2023) and the "new" cross-border worker. Old cross-border workers benefit from an exemption of €7,500 annually until 2033, while new ones have a threshold of €10,000. These amounts refer to the income declared in Italy (model 730 or Unico, CE section). A change in the canton of work does not invalidate these rights, but it must be reported to the employer so that they update the documentation with the cantonal tax office. At the time of the annual declaration, the situation must remain consistent: if a cross-border worker declares working in a different canton from the previous one, the refunds (calculated through the Italy tax credit in the CE section) may vary due to different cantonal rates, but the methodology remains the same. [Discover how to manage the income tax declaration](nav:tax-return). Italy compensates the tax already paid in Switzerland through the ordinary model 730 or the standard income tax declaration, ensuring the absence of double taxation.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Operational procedure: checklist for changing canton
Before submitting your resignation, or immediately after signing the new contract, the cross-border worker must verify some fundamental points. First, communicate in writing to the previous employer the transition to a new employer: the end-of-relationship documentation must specify the end date and the amount of TFR (End-of-Employment Compensation), or the Swiss equivalent if already paid. Request a copy of the communication that the new employer will make to the AFC and SEM (within 8 days from the first day of work) and verify that the G Permit is correctly registered with the new canton of employment.
Subsequently, check that the new employer has enrolled the cross-border worker in the AVS, LPP, and accident insurance funds of the new canton. Request a copy of the enrollment notification to the funds. If coming from a previous Swiss enrollment, verify the transfer of acquired LPP rights (if portable according to the fund's regulations). Notify the change of canton to the LAMal insurer within two weeks of the change of work address. If you intend to change insurer, cancel at least 3 months before the annual policy expiration.
Check the amounts withheld in the first pay slip of the new canton: withholding tax, AVS, LPP, and health insurance. Compare them with the previous pay slip to ensure they align with the tax tables of the new canton. If you notice any anomalies, report them immediately to the new employer.
### Critical deadlines and documents
The income tax return in Italy (model 730 or Unico) must be submitted by September 30 of the year following the tax period. For a canton change occurring during the year, the transition year declaration must clearly indicate both employers and their respective work periods, so that the calculation of refunds (tax credit, CE section of the 730) is correct. Keep the monthly pay slip from both employers, along with official communications on payments to Swiss funds. If the change occurs in the first months of the year (January-March), register the new work permit with the Italian municipalities of residence: it serves as documentary support in case of tax checks on the correct declaration of income.
After gathering information on the new canton, the new gross salary, and the estimated contributions from the new employer, calculate the expected net income by comparing it with the previous one. [Use the salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the pay slip in both cantons and evaluate the real impact of the change. In parallel, if you wish to consult the LAMal options suitable in the new canton, refer to the insurance guide to verify deductibles and premiums. Finally, keep all documentation (contracts, pay slips, AFC communications, enrollment confirmations to funds) for the income tax return of the transition year.

item.description: Border crossing from Gravedona and the United States to Ticino: taxation, permits, New Agreement, contributions and what to evaluate before moving.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Living in Italy (Gravedona) and working in Switzerland (Ticino): cross-border regime with G permit - Withholding tax deducted in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy (form 730, section CE) - New Cross-Border Agreement from January 1, 2024: exemption CHF 7,500 (old) or CHF 10,000 (new) - AVS/LPP/LAMal: mandatory Swiss contributions and social security for cross-border workers
## Key facts - **What**: New Cross-Border Agreement between Italy and Switzerland with tax exemption regimes - When: Signed on December 23, 2020, effective from January 1, 2024 (Law 83/2023 IT) - Where: Cross-border workers Como-Ticino, residents in Italy, workers in Switzerland - Exemption amount: CHF 7,500 for old cross-border workers (registered before 17/7/2023), CHF 10,000 for new ones - Tax: Deducted solely in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy - Double taxation agreement: Signed on December 9, 1976, prevents double taxation - Permit: G permit for cross-border workers (seasonal 4-12 months), issued by SEM (Migration Section) - LAMal: Cross-border workers with G permit have the option between Swiss LAMal and Italian CMI
Living in Gravedona ed Uniti, in the province of Como, and working in Ticino as a cross-border worker means adhering to specific tax rules, permits, and social security. The New Cross-Border Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and effective from January 1, 2024 (Italian ratification: Law 83 of June 13, 2023), has established the tax regime for cross-border commuters. The withholding tax is deducted solely in Switzerland, while in Italy, the tax credit is applied through form 730 (section CE). For old cross-border workers, already registered before July 17, 2023, an exemption of CHF 7,500 applies with a transitional regime until 2033. New cross-border workers benefit from a CHF 10,000 allowance. These elements determine the net monthly salary and must be carefully evaluated before choosing Gravedona as a residential base.
### G Permit and cross-border residence
To live in Gravedona ed Uniti and work in Ticino, the cross-border worker must have a G permit (seasonal 4-12 months) or actual residence in Switzerland (B permit). The G permit is issued by the Migration Section (SEM) and allows the exercise of dependent activity in Switzerland while maintaining residence in Italy. Choosing to reside in Gravedona, in the province of Como, places the cross-border worker in a specific Italy-Switzerland tax regime regulated by the Double Taxation Agreement signed on December 9, 1976. This agreement ensures that employment income is taxed solely in the country of employment (Switzerland), avoiding double taxation.
### Taxation: withholding tax and tax credit
The withholding tax on employment income is deducted solely by Switzerland. Italy does not apply additional taxes on employment income for cross-border workers with a G permit but allows the recovery of the tax credit in form 730 (section CE), summing the Swiss tax paid and the worldwide income declared in Italy. Swiss federal rates vary based on the canton and personal conditions; the Canton of Ticino applies specific brackets. There is no double taxation but a single payment in Switzerland and partial recovery in Italy. This mechanism is crucial for planning the net salary and expected annual taxes.
### Social contributions and pensions
A cross-border worker residing in Gravedona and working in Ticino pays Swiss social contributions. AVS/AI (old-age and disability insurance) involves a 5.3% rate for the employee, while the employer pays the same percentage. Unemployment insurance (AD/AC) is 1.1% (employee) up to an annual salary limit of CHF 148,200. Accident insurance (LAINF) is 0.7-1.5%. These contributions are mandatory and feed the Swiss pension system (first pillar AVS) and professional pension (second pillar LPP), where the employee pays a share between 7% and 18% depending on the age group (mandatory from the 25th year of life). To learn more about planning your [future pension](nav:pension) and understanding AVS/LPP, consult our dedicated tools. In Italy, the cross-border worker DOES NOT pay additional INPS contributions for Swiss employment income, but the Swiss contribution career counts for the Italian pension through the totalization of contribution periods between the two countries. ### Health Insurance and Choice Between LAMal and CMI
A border worker with Permit G can choose to insure with a Swiss health insurance fund (LAMal) or maintain Italian coverage (CMI). This right of choice is enshrined in the New Border Workers Agreement. If they opt for LAMal, they will choose a deductible between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 (adults). If they remain with CMI, they maintain the basic Italian coverage (SSN) and can supplement it with additional policies. The choice has implications for the monthly cost and the network of hospitals that can be used (Ticino hospitals vs. Lombardy hospitals). Many border workers from Como who live in Gravedona choose CMI to maintain continuity with doctors and hospitals in the province.
### Border Workers Agreement and Transitional Regimes
The New Border Workers Agreement, in force from January 1, 2024, introduces income brackets with temporary tax exemptions. Border workers already registered before July 17, 2023 (old border workers) benefit from an annual exemption of CHF 7,500 within a transitional regime that covers the decade 2024–2033. New border workers (registered from July 17, 2023 onwards) have access to an annual exemption of CHF 10,000 without a time limit. This difference directly impacts the Swiss taxable income and, consequently, the withholding tax. A border worker resident in Gravedona must verify their registration as an old or new border worker with their Ticino employer or with the Swiss tax authorities (AFC, Federal Tax Administration). The status determines the annual tax savings.
### Border Crossings and Connection to Ticino
Gravedona ed Uniti is located in the province of Como, not far from the main border crossings with Ticino (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa). The proximity to the crossings is a decisive factor in the choice of residence, as it affects daily travel times and the practicality of commuting. Each border worker should check the current schedules of public transport (trains, buses) and traffic conditions at the crossings before signing a lease or purchase contract. Additionally, a [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) on our site allows you to simulate the impact of withholding tax and Swiss contributions on the monthly net salary by entering the gross salary and border worker status. Furthermore, a [CHF/EUR comparator](nav:exchange) allows you to evaluate the currency exchange rate to plan the monthly budget in a bilateral perspective.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step 1: Check your status as an old or new frontier worker
Before moving to Gravedona, it is essential to determine whether you are an 'old frontier worker' (registered before July 17, 2023) or a 'new frontier worker' (registered from July 17, 2023 onwards). This status directly impacts your tax exemption (CHF 7,500 vs. CHF 10,000). Contact your Ticino employer or the Swiss tax authorities (AFC, Federal Tax Administration) to confirm your status. This is not a given and can make a difference of hundreds of francs per year on Swiss federal taxation.
### Step 2: Choose your health insurance scheme
Within the terms set by the New Agreement, decide whether to join LAMal (Swiss) or maintain CMI (Italian). This choice affects your monthly premium, deductible, and available healthcare network. If you choose LAMal, select the deductible that best suits your profile (CHF 300-2,500 for adults). If you stay with CMI, ensure that your Italian coverage is sufficient for care in Switzerland (emergency hospitalization). Contact providers of both systems to compare monthly costs and included services.
### Step 3: Plan your annual tax return
A frontier worker residing in Gravedona must complete two annual tax returns: in Switzerland with the Ticino cantonal tax authorities (if the canton requires a return), and in Italy using form 730 or 1040 (if without an employer CUD) in section CE (foreign tax credit), attaching Swiss tax statements. This procedure is mandatory annually and allows you to reclaim the tax credit and verify that double taxation has not been applied. Consulting a tax specialist in frontier workers is recommended, as calculating the tax credit requires precision and knowledge of the Italy-Switzerland treaties.
### Step 4: Register with the Municipality of Gravedona
Once you have found accommodation in Gravedona ed Uniti, register with the municipal registry as a resident. This is mandatory under Italian law. The Municipality will issue a residence certificate, essential for obtaining a tax code (if not already in possession), for opening bank accounts, for registering your employment contract with INPS (even though the work is in Switzerland), and for other Italian administrative procedures. The declared residence is the legal starting point for all cross-border tax and pension management.
### Tools for financial planning
The overview of the New Frontier Workers Agreement, the Italo-Swiss tax system, and mandatory pension schemes is complex, but addressing it before moving to Gravedona is essential. Every frontier worker should take the time to understand withholding tax, tax credit, exemption brackets, and the Swiss pension system (AVS/LPP/LAMal) before signing an employment contract. Use our [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your net salary based on your frontier worker status and gross salary: it is the first concrete step in planning your move to Gravedona and employment in Ticino.

item.title: Varese: over 20,000 without a doctor, a challenge for border workers
item.description: Over 20,000 residents without a doctor in Varese. In two years 92 retired doctors. A crisis that affects Ticino border workers residing in the province.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - 15,177 patients without a doctor in Asst Sette Laghi: immediate emergency - 4,983 patients without a doctor in Asst Valle Olona with 92 doctors retiring - Shortage persists for over 2 years in some districts; temporary clinics cover the emergency
## Key facts - **What**: Severe shortage of general practitioners in the province of Varese - Where: Asst Sette Laghi (15,177 citizens) and Asst Valle Olona (4,983 citizens) - When: 2026-2027; 17 doctors retiring in Sette Laghi, 92 in Valle Olona by the end of 2027 - Who: PD councilor Samuele Astuti raised the alarm through access to documents - Impact: Over 20,160 citizens without a stable reference for primary healthcare
Over 20,000 citizens in the province of Varese do not have a general practitioner. This is the alarming picture that emerges from official data provided by the two local health and social care companies following an access to documents presented by the regional councilor of the Democratic Party Samuele Astuti. In total, 15,177 patients are uncovered in Asst Sette Laghi, while 4,983 are in Asst Valle Olona, for a total of over 20,160 residents without a stable figure for primary healthcare.
The situation does not represent a temporary emergency but a chronic shortage that has now lasted for years. In the Gazzada district, for example, the difficulty has persisted for about two years: uncovered patients in Daverio must turn to the temporary clinic in Gazzada to obtain essential prescriptions and visits. The province of Varese is geographically significant for Ticino-Italy commuters: many of them reside in the municipalities of Varesotto (Varese, Busto Arsizio, Gallarate, Saronno, Somma Lombardo, Azzate, Luino, Tradate, Arcisate) and are directly affected by this daily shortage. For those living on the Swiss-Italian border and working in Ticino, the lack of a stable doctor represents a concrete obstacle in managing healthcare continuity.
### The wave of retirements in the next two years
Adding to the complexity, a massive wave of retirements is already planned. In Asst Sette Laghi, 17 doctors will reach retirement age by the end of 2027. Specifically, four doctors will cease activity by the end of 2026: one in the Sesto Calende district, one in Tradate, two in the Varese district. During 2027, another thirteen professionals will leave the activity (two in Arcisate, three in Azzate, one in Laveno Mombello, two in Luino, two in Tradate, three in Varese).
The situation in Asst Valle Olona is even more critical. There are 37 doctors who will reach 70 years by the end of 2026 and another 55 by the end of 2027, for a total of 92 professionals potentially leaving within two years. Not all will necessarily leave the activity as soon as they meet the requirements, but the data clearly reveals the scale of the generational turnover that will need to be addressed to contain the crisis. Districts such as Gallarate and Busto Arsizio will see a particular concentration: ten doctors in Gallarate by the end of 2026, another fourteen by the end of 2027; fourteen in Busto Arsizio-Castellanza by the end of 2026, another twenty-one by the end of 2027.
### The limits of temporary medical clinics
Temporary medical clinics allow for the provision of prescriptions, urgent visits, and essential medical certificates. However, they represent a response born to manage the emergency that risks becoming the ordinary mode of access to care. For elderly patients, people with chronic diseases, and vulnerable subjects—including many elderly commuters—the continuity with a family doctor is essential. Without it, the quality of primary healthcare suffers a significant decline. ## What it means for the border worker resident in Varese
Ticino-Italy border workers who reside in the province of Varese are in a particularly delicate situation. This group of workers resides in Italy and works in Switzerland: a geographical configuration that exposes them to the problems of Italian health, but which also allows them to access the Swiss health system. The shortage of primary care physicians in Varese is not a purely local issue-it is a concrete problem that impacts the continuity of care, especially for elderly border workers or those with established chronic diseases.
A stable general practitioner provides diagnostic continuity, knows the patient's medical history, coordinates any specialist examinations and provides medical certificates necessary for work and administrative procedures in Switzerland. When this figure is missing, the border worker must resort to temporary surgeries, which guarantee the essential services (request for medicines, urgent visits, short-term certificates) but not the relational and diagnostic continuity that characterizes family medicine. The lack of continuity is particularly problematic for those who have to coordinate their health between two health systems - the Italian one of residence and the Swiss one of work.
### Deadlines and numbers to keep an eye on
By the end of 2026, four doctors from Asst Seven Lakes will have reached pension requirements.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## What to do if you are a resident of Varesotto without a family doctor
If you live in Varesotto and do not have a stable general practitioner, your immediate options are two: access the temporary clinic of your district or, if you have a G permit (cross-border worker), consider enrolling in the Swiss healthcare system as a structural alternative.
1. **Contact the relevant ASST** (Sette Laghi or Valle Olona depending on your district) to find out the location and hours of the temporary clinic in your area. 2. Bring essential documentation: national health card, identity document. 3. Obtain essential services: prescriptions for medications, urgent visits, medical certificates for a short period. 4. Request guidance for specialists: the temporary clinic can provide indications on how to access specialist visits if necessary.
The procedure is simplified, but remember that temporary clinics do not replace the family doctor: they do not have access to your previous medical history, cannot manage chronic conditions continuously, and the service is limited to the most urgent services. For the cross-border worker, this solution represents a temporary measure, not a cure.
### Alternative option for the cross-border worker: access to the Swiss healthcare system
If you have a G permit (cross-border worker), you have the right to choose whether to insure yourself with a Swiss health insurance (LAMal) or to maintain enrollment in the Italian healthcare service. This right is called the 'right of option'. If you choose to insure yourself in Switzerland, you will be able to access Swiss family doctors and benefit from the Swiss healthcare system, ensuring continuity of care even during periods of work in Ticino.
For the cross-border worker residing in Varesotto who works in Ticino, this option allows you to bypass the shortage of Italian doctors and ensure structural continuity of care through the Swiss system. However, this choice involves significant fiscal and administrative implications: it entails the obligation to pay different AVS/AI contributions, determines a change in the tax regime for income taxation, and affects declarations to Italian authorities. Check the documentation related to the cross-border option at the Italian Revenue Agency or contact a professional specializing in cross-border taxation directly.
### Monitoring the system in 2026-2027
The situation in the next 12-18 months could significantly worsen: the flow of retirements is already scheduled, and the Lombardy Region has not yet communicated a structural generational replacement strategy. Periodically monitor the communications of the relevant ASST to understand if: - New doctors are being recruited and when they will start their activity - Temporary clinics will remain available or will undergo reductions in hours - Your geographical area (district) will receive priority in recruitment - New planning measures are announced by the Lombardy Region
Periodically check the website of ASST Sette Laghi or Valle Olona (depending on where you reside) in the section dedicated to territorial medicine and enrollment with family doctors. Some municipalities manage the updated list of available doctors directly.
### Concrete steps: planning your healthcare coverage
In parallel with monitoring actions, plan your healthcare strategy: - If you have chronic conditions, make sure to obtain prescriptions from the temporary clinic with extended validity; - If you work in Ticino and need medical certificates for absence from work, clarify in advance with your employer which entities are recognized in Switzerland (generally, Italian certificates are not automatically valid in CH); - If you are considering the option of enrolling in LAMal, contact at least two Swiss insurers to understand the costs and available coverage in your situation.
The shortage of doctors in Varesotto is a structural problem affecting the entire province, but with the right information and careful planning of your healthcare coverage, you can ensure continuity of your care. [Consult our calculator](nav:calculator) to understand how a choice of enrollment in LAMal could affect your fiscal situation as a cross-border worker.
*Source: [varesenews.it](https://www.varesenews.it/2026/09/oltre-20mila-cittadini-senza-medico-di-base-nel-varesotto-e-incombe-londata-dei-pensionamenti/2669674/)*

item.title: Frontier changes canton: the tax implications
item.description: Canton change = new taxation, modified G permit and different commuter costs. Practical guide for border workers in transition between Ticino and Grisons.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Changing canton requires modification of the G permit and notification to SECO and the destination canton - Withholding tax remains exclusively in Switzerland (no double taxation) - Old cross-border workers keep the €7,500 exemption until 2033; new ones receive a €10,000 allowance
## Key facts - **What**: Change of canton of work for cross-border workers (e.g., Ticino → Grisons) and administrative procedures - When: From 1 January 2024 (new Cross-Border Workers Agreement in force) - Where: From Canton Ticino to Grisons or other Swiss cantons - Who: Cross-border workers regulated by Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Amount: Withholding tax retained solely in Switzerland; exemption €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) - Legislation: New Cross-Border Workers Agreement (23 December 2020, Italian-Swiss Convention 9 December 1976)
Changing the canton of work for an Italian cross-border worker is not a simple contractual modification. It involves revisions to the G permit, adjustments to withholding tax, and checks on administrative deadlines with the competent authorities. Unlike what is sometimes assumed, the withholding tax on employment income remains exclusively in Switzerland. There is no 'double taxation in both countries': Italy avoids double taxation by using the foreign tax credit in the CE section of the income tax return (model 730).
The transition between cantons involves administrative searches with SECO (Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs), USTAT (Ticino Statistical Office), and the competent cantonal tax administrations, especially to verify communication times. From 1 January 2024, the procedures for this transition are formalized according to the regulatory framework of Law 83 of 13 June 2023.
### G Permit and Change of Canton The condition of the G permit (cross-border work authorization) is linked to the place of employment and the duration of the contract. A change of canton does not automatically invalidate the permit but requires timely notification to the competent authorities: in Switzerland to SECO and the destination canton (e.g., Grisons), in Italy to INPS through a declaration by the new employer. If the transition occurs at the beginning of the calendar year, notifications must already be made in December of the previous year. The cross-border worker does not submit applications but is the responsibility of the Swiss employer to manage the authorization procedure with the federal and cantonal authorities.
### Withholding Tax: What Does NOT Change Many cross-border workers believe that changing cantons involves a 'recalculation of withholding tax from scratch.' Instead, the rate is set by the canton of employment based on marital status, annualized gross income, and specific exemptions. It remains retained solely in Switzerland. According to the new 2024 agreement, old cross-border workers (already employed before 17 July 2023) keep the €7,500 exemption, with a transitional regime until 2033. New cross-border workers benefit from a €10,000 allowance. The continuity of the exemption is guaranteed by Law 83/2023, regardless of the change of canton. The change of canton is not instantaneous from a tax and administrative point of view. Communication to the new canton and cancellation of registration in the previous canton require a lag of 1-3 months, depending on the speed of the cantonal authorities. During this transitional period, the cross-border worker may receive two pay slips: one from the old canton (with termination of the relationship) and one from the new canton (with start of employment). It is essential to keep all pay slips from both periods for the annual declaration: the INPS and the Italian Revenue Agency will have to reconcile the periods of employment in order to avoid double deductions or contribution gaps.
### Variations in cantonal taxation between Ticino and Grisons
The cantonal withholding tax rates vary considerably between Ticino and Grisons. Although both are Swiss cantons, the cantonal withholding tax can differ by 2-3 percentage points, at the same gross income. A cross-border worker moving from Ticino to Grisons does not experience 'double taxation': the new canton simply applies its rate from the first day of employment. No 'retroactive recovery' from the old canton.
However, variations in local allowances or in the calculation of pension contributions (AVS/AI/IPG for employee: 5.3%; AD/AC: 1.1%; LAINF: 0.7-1.5%; LPP for age group from 25 years: 7-18%) can affect the net pay slip. The SUVA (Swiss National Accident Insurance Institute) has a standardized national taxation, while the LPP (professional pension insurance) is managed by cantonal funds: the new employer in Grisons may have an LPP fund with slightly different rates compared to the previous Ticino fund.
### Impact of commuting on costs and border crossings
The change of canton from Ticino to Grisons implies a completely different commuting route. If the cross-border worker works in Lugano or Mendrisio (Ticino), he normally uses the Brogeda border crossing (Ticino-Italy border) or Gaggiolo. Moving to Grisons (for example, Chur or Davos), the route changes: the commuter may use different border crossings or routes, with implications for transit times, car vignette costs, and tax deductibility of transport costs. In Italy, the costs incurred to reach the cross-border workplace are partially deductible from the model 730, but only if documented and consistent with the verified route.
Furthermore, if the change of canton implies a change of residence in Italy (for example, from Como to Sondrio), a coordination issue arises between Swiss legislation (G permit linked to the workplace) and Italian legislation (tax residence linked to residence). The Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976 provides that employment income is taxable in the country where it is performed — and therefore remains in Switzerland — but the Italian tax residence must be updated with the Municipality and subsequently with the Revenue Agency.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Administrative checklist: step-by-step cantonal change
1. Communication to the new employer (Grisons): The new Swiss employer (Grisons) must submit a G permit request and a notice of employment to the SECO and the competent cantonal authority. This communication is the responsibility of the employer, not the cross-border commuter, but the commuter must ensure that the employer is aware of the procedure and deadlines.
2. Revocation of the G permit from the old canton (Ticino): Simultaneously, the previous Ticino employer communicates the termination of the employment relationship to the Ticino authorities. The revocation is automatic if the relationship ends, but it may take 2-4 weeks to be processed by the cantonal administrations.
3. **Notification to INPS**: The new Swiss employer notifies INPS (Italian side) of the cantonal change within the legal deadlines. In Italy, this notification is made through the 'Visura INPS' form or equivalent, to ensure the continuity of pension contributions.
4. Update with the Tax Agency: If the cross-border commuter has changed their Italian tax residence (e.g., moving residence), they must notify the municipality of residence (registry office) and subsequently the Tax Agency through the 'AA9/12' form or equivalent.
5. Verification of the exemption threshold: If the cross-border commuter is an 'old cross-border commuter' (employed before July 17, 2023), they retain the €7,500 exemption with a transitional regime until 2033. If they are a 'new cross-border commuter', the threshold is €10,000. This information should be verified with the new employer and the Grisons cantonal administration.
6. LAMal: right of option for health insurance: The cross-border commuter with a G permit has the right to choose between Swiss health insurance (LAMal) or to remain in the Italian system (CMI/SSN). If they stay in Italy, they do not pay Swiss LAMal contributions. If they opt for LAMal, they must communicate their choice to the new employer and the Grisons health insurance fund. The adult deductibles in LAMal range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 per year.
### Critical deadlines
- Before the change: communicate the termination date to the previous employer with notice according to the Swiss national contract (usually 1-3 months). - Within the month before the new position: verify that the new employer has submitted the permit request to the SECO. - Within 30 days from the start of the relationship: the new canton must confirm the authorization. - Within 90 days: all notifications must be processed (INPS, Tax Agency).
To verify the impact on withholding tax with the new Grisons cantonal rate, use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) — simulate the pay slip based on gross income and the new cross-border status. If you have doubts about double taxation or managing the tax return with the new canton, consult the [guide to cross-border refunds](nav:ristorni), which explains how the foreign tax credit works on the 730 form. To evaluate whether the cantonal change is convenient compared to alternatives, the [G permit comparator](nav:permits) helps to assess whether a different solution (e.g., moving residence and B permit) is more advantageous.

item.title: Swiss road fines: payment from an Italian resident
item.description: How does the notification and payment of a Swiss traffic fine for an Italian resident work? Procedures, terms, appeals and implications for Permit G.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - An Italian resident receives a Swiss traffic fine notification by mail at their Italian address - Payment and appeals are regulated by the competent cantonal administrative procedure - Non-payment leads to administrative escalation and possible impacts on car insurance - The Italian-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976 protects the appeal rights of cross-border commuters
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss traffic fine notified to an Italian resident - Location: Swiss territory (violation) → notification in Italy (home address) - Authority: Competent cantonal administrative offices for traffic sanctions - Right: Right to appeal within the deadline indicated in the notice - Agreement: Italian-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976 regulates procedures - SEM: State Secretariat for Migration evaluates the behavior of cross-border commuters
An Italian cross-border commuter who drives in Switzerland and receives a traffic fine does not get it notified at the traffic light. Instead, the notice arrives weeks later, by ordinary or registered mail, directly to their home in Italy. This is the first critical element that Italian residents often do not know: Switzerland relies on the home address to contact the driver, and this (for a cross-border commuter) is in Italy, not in Switzerland.
The sanctioning procedure is regulated by the competent Swiss cantonal authorities for the territory where the violation occurred. If the fine concerns the Canton of Ticino or the Grisons (cantons bordering Italy), the notification will travel directly to the Italian resident's municipality. The notice always contains: - the description of the violation (speeding, red light, irregular parking, phone while driving, failure to use a seatbelt, etc.) - the date, time, and exact location of the violation - the amount of the fine determined by Swiss law - the deadline for payment - precise instructions for filing an appeal - the name of the responsible authority and contact details
### Notification channel and deadlines
Notification occurs by official mail. There is no real-time notification via app or email; even cantons that develop digital systems maintain mail as the official channel. The cross-border commuter must regularly check their mailbox: missing the receipt of the notification DOES NOT cancel the payment obligation. Administrative silence, instead, turns into a more serious legal problem over time.
Upon receiving the notification, the cross-border commuter has a specific deadline (indicated in the Swiss document) for two options: 1. Pay the fine before the deadline (by depositing via Swiss postal account or bank transfer) 2. File an appeal with the competent authority if they do not agree with the infraction
If they do not act within the deadline, Switzerland takes forced collection measures. Maintaining a [cross-border commuter permit](nav:permits) also requires compliance with Swiss laws, so ignoring a fine could have indirect consequences on the recognition of the right to work in Switzerland. For the cross-border worker, receiving a Swiss traffic fine has implications beyond the fine itself. The first is the civil liability insurance (RC auto). If the violation caused damage (accident), the insurance company may deny coverage or increase the premium at the next renewal. The [cost of car insurance](nav:car-cost) for those who frequently drive in Switzerland for work reasons is a significant part of the cross-border worker's budget: a history of violations can increase the premium cost by 20-30%. The second implication concerns the [Permit G](nav:permits), the cross-border worker's permit. The Permit G is linked to the exercise of a professional activity in Switzerland (almost always employment). A traffic fine alone DOES NOT revoke the permit, but if accompanied by more serious offenses (driving without insurance, extreme speeding above legal limits, repeated offenses), it could attract the attention of the SEM authorities (State Secretariat for Migration). The SEM periodically evaluates the cross-border worker's behavior in Switzerland to decide whether to keep the permit valid. If the payment is ignored The non-payment within the deadline does not make the fine disappear. Instead, the amount increases. Switzerland adds administrative penalties for the delay and can proceed with forced debt recovery through the Italian residence. In some cases, the unpaid fine could prevent the renewal of the driver's license or create problems in the vehicle registers (e.g., blocking circulation in Switzerland until payment). A common scenario: the cross-border worker receives the notice, ignores it thinking that in Italy it will not have legal consequences, and then discovers years later that the fine is still open with surcharges, and that they can no longer legally drive in Switzerland.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). If you have received a Swiss traffic fine, here is what to do concretively:
1. **Read the notice completely**. Verify that your data is correct, that the date and place of the violation correspond to the facts. If you find errors (wrong license plate, incorrect date), these are valid reasons for appeal.
2. Decide whether to pay or appeal. If you recognize the violation and want to close the case quickly, pay within the indicated deadline (usually 30 days from when you receive the notice). If you disagree, prepare a written appeal explaining your reasons.
3. If you pay: transfer the amount via Swiss postal account (the number is on the notice) or bank transfer. Keep the payment receipt. Once paid, the case is closed.
4. If you appeal: send a letter to the authority indicated in the notice. Explain why you think the fine is unjust (e.g., the speed limit was not clear, the traffic light was defective, etc.). Include photos, witnesses, or any evidence. Send everything by registered mail and keep the receipt.
### Appeals and Rights
The right of appeal is guaranteed by Swiss laws and protected by the Italo-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976. If your appeal is rejected, you can further escalate the case to the cantonal administrative court, but this requires specialized legal assistance (lawyer with knowledge of the bilateral CH-IT systems and Swiss administrative law).
For specific advice on the fine, contact a Ticino consumer association or a law firm that knows the bilateral CH-IT systems. Many professionals offer free initial consultations to assess the strength of the appeal.
Use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to evaluate how the fine and any potential insurance premium increases affect your overall situation as a cross-border worker.
